content: Receding gums, also known as gingival recession, describe the loss of gum tissue that leads to the exposure of the roots of the teeth. This condition is commonly observed in adults over the age of 40, although it can begin as early as the teenage years. Causes of Receding Gums: 1. Overaggressive Brushing: Excessive force during toothbrushing can lead to gum recession. This occurs when the enamel at the gum line is worn away due to a scrubbing motion, often described as a washboard effect. 2. Inadequate Brushing or Flossing: Poor oral hygiene allows bacteria to accumulate between the teeth. The enzymes released by these bacteria can erode the bone supporting the teeth, which is highly detrimental to oral health. 3. Periodontal Disease: Gum recession can also result from periodontal (gum) disease, a chronic inflammatory condition that damages the supporting structures of the teeth. 4. Use of Smokeless Tobacco (Snuff): Placing snuff between the lip and teeth can damage the mucous membrane lining of the mouth, leading to gum recession over time. 5. Improper Placement of Lip or Tongue Piercings: Poorly positioned oral piercings can irritate and damage the gums, contributing to recession. Treatment of Receding Gums: Treatment begins by addressing the underlying cause of the gum recession: If overaggressive brushing is the cause, patients should switch to a softer toothbrush and adopt a gentler brushing technique. If poor plaque control is a factor, improved oral hygiene practices, combined with regular professional dental cleanings (prophylaxis), are essential. In cases where severe tartar (calculus) buildup is present, a procedure called scaling and root planing may be required. This involves deep cleaning to remove tartar and reduce inflammation in the gums. Gum (Gingival) Grafting: In more advanced cases, gum recession can be treated with a surgical procedure known as gum grafting or periodontal plastic surgery. The choice of technique depends on the extent of the recession and the amount of bone support around the teeth. These procedures are typically performed by a periodontist (a specialist in gum health) under local anesthesia, with or without conscious sedation, depending on the patient’s preference. Pedicle Graft: This involves repositioning adjacent gum tissue to cover the exposed root. Free Gingival Graft or Connective Tissue Graft: Tissue is harvested from the roof of the patient’s mouth (palate) and used to cover the recession area. Acellular Dermal Matrix: In some cases, processed donated human skin (allograft) is used instead of the patient’s own tissue. Healing from these procedures generally takes 2 to 4 weeks. After a few months, the results are evaluated, and in some cases, minor reshaping of the new tissue may be performed to achieve optimal outcomes. When gum recession is not accompanied by significant bone loss, complete or near-complete coverage of the affected area is often achievable.
